review: Source/resolved judgments re-read directly. Moral question wrongly characterized biblical examples as divine commands and Horn access as revelation; faculty reply invented sacrificial heroism/distortion and substituted grounding criticism; hiddenness omitted actual unsupported auxiliary prior-cost cancellation and introduced prevalence criticism. Same authorized leaves require correction; no submission occurred.

cards.words: Lataster questions whether moral intuitions reliably disclose objective facts, using biblical commands involving rape and genocide to challenge Horn’s confidence in divinely grounded moral knowledge.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Lataster targets the epistemic bridge rather than merely repeating ontological doubt, using morally troubling biblical commands to test whether claimed revelation and intuition reliably track the objective standards Horn invokes. Principal limitation: Disagreement and contested scriptural interpretation do not themselves establish subjectivism, error theory, or the unreliability of every moral judgment, and the compressed question supplies no developed alternative epistemology. Live burden: He must explain how these examples should reduce confidence in Horn’s access claim without assuming that uncertainty about particular judgments defeats moral realism as such. Locked score: 76 The challenge is pointed, relevant, and responsive because it pressures a genuine warrant, but its rhetorical compression and limited positive account prevent the examples from supporting the broader skeptical implications Lataster sometimes suggests.

cards.words: Horn replies that humans possess a natural moral faculty whose judgments can be distorted, using near-universal admiration for sacrificial heroism to illustrate agreement despite moral error.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Horn offers a coherent faculty model explaining how objective moral knowledge can coexist with distortion and identifies sacrificial heroism as a concrete case of broad evaluative agreement. Principal limitation: One compelling example does not establish the reliability of the faculty generally, and his claim of near-universal agreement is broader and more confident than the illustration supports. Live burden: He must justify the faculty’s trustworthiness and connect its deliverances to divine grounding rather than merely showing that disagreement is compatible with objective truth; the later cannibalism context creates no penalty for an earlier unmade reply. Locked score: 74 The response is intelligible and relevant to the epistemic objection, but its narrow evidence, overstated consensus, and unfinished metaphysical bridge substantially restrict its evidential warrant and calibration.

cards.words: Lataster presents suffering and nonresistant nonbelief as evidence less expected under a loving, knowing, powerful God, while expressly denying that either consideration logically disproves every deity.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Lataster frames suffering and hiddenness as comparative evidence against the specified relational and perfectly good deity, carefully distinguishing reduced probability from a deductive claim that no God can exist. Principal limitation: The move does not yet establish how unexpected the observations are under classical theism, how frequently nonresistant nonbelief occurs, or which alternative hypothesis predicts the combined evidence better. Live burden: He must defend the relevant likelihood contrast and address plausible divine reasons, while Horn must do more than establish logical compatibility because a possible explanation does not determine comparative expectation. Locked score: 81 The argument is highly relevant, coherent, and well calibrated to the negative burden, but incomplete likelihood support and limited empirical development prevent its probabilistic conclusion from receiving stronger evidential credit.
